title: Type Conversions & Casting
summary: Go has **no implicit numeric conversions** — you must write `T(v)` explicitly, even between `int` and `int64`. This strictness eliminates a whole class of C-style bugs, but it also means you need to understand truncation, overflow, and the famous `string(65)` gotcha to convert values correctly.

subtopics.title: Explicit conversion T(v)
subtopics.explanation: Go never converts numeric types implicitly. To use an int where an int64 is expected you must write the conversion yourself: int64(x). The compiler rejects mixing types, which catches accidental data-truncation bugs at compile time rather than at runtime. This explicit T(v) syntax is the single rule the whole topic of conversions is built on.

subtopics.title: int <-> float64 truncates
subtopics.explanation: Converting a float to an int truncates toward zero — it does NOT round. So int(2.9) is 2 and int(-2.9) is -2. Converting int to float64 is exact for small magnitudes but can lose precision for very large integers. This truncation is one of the surprises an explicit conversion can hide if you expect rounding.

subtopics.title: Narrowing overflows predictably
subtopics.explanation: Converting a wide integer to a narrower one keeps only the low bits — well-defined two's-complement truncation, not undefined behavior. int8(300) wraps to 44. Always check range before narrowing untrusted values. This is a conversion whose result can silently corrupt data when the value doesn't fit the target type.

subtopics.title: string(n) is the rune gotcha
subtopics.explanation: string(65) is "A", not "65" — converting an integer to a string interprets it as a Unicode code point. To get the decimal text use strconv.Itoa(65). Modern Go vet even warns about int-to-string conversions. This is the most famous conversion trap the T(v) rule exposes.

subtopics.title: []byte / []rune copy the data
subtopics.explanation: []byte(s) and []rune(s) allocate a new slice and copy, because strings are immutable. string([]byte{...}) round-trips back. These conversions are not free — avoid them in hot loops. Unlike numeric conversions, these string conversions allocate, so they are the costly members of the conversion family.

subtopics.title: Defined types & their underlying type
subtopics.explanation: A defined type like type Celsius float64 is distinct from float64; you must convert explicitly between them (Celsius(t) / float64(c)) even though they share representation. This gives you type safety with no runtime cost. It is the same explicit-conversion rule applied to your own domain types, not just built-in numbers.

foundations.overview: Many languages quietly convert one numeric type to another for you — an int becomes a double, a char becomes an int — and that convenience hides bugs. Go takes the opposite stance: it has NO implicit numeric conversions. If two values are of different types, you must convert one explicitly with the T(v) syntax. This lesson covers the rules: how numeric conversions truncate and overflow, why string(65) is a famous trap, and how strconv handles real number-to-text work.
foundations.formalDefinition: A conversion T(x) changes the type of an expression x to the type T when x is assignable to T or their underlying types are convertible. It is a compile-time, value-producing operation distinct from a type assertion, which is a runtime check on an interface value.
foundations.whyItMatters: Conversions sit at every boundary: parsing input, talking to databases, serializing JSON, doing math across types. Getting them wrong silently corrupts data — a truncated float, an overflowed counter, or a byte that turns into a Chinese character instead of '42'.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of each type as a labeled box of a fixed size. T(v) means 'take the bits in this box and reinterpret/repackage them into a T-shaped box.' Sometimes that fits perfectly (int to int64), sometimes it must drop bits (int64 to int8), and sometimes it reinterprets meaning entirely (int to string treats the number as a code point).
commonUseCases: Parsing text input with strconv.Atoi / strconv.Itoa
Bridging int and int64 at API/DB boundaries
Building []byte payloads from strings for I/O
Defining domain types (type UserID int64) for safety

commonMisconceptions.reality: It gives the rune for code point 42 (a control character). Use strconv.Itoa(42) for the decimal text "42".
Numeric conversions are cheap, but []byte(s), []rune(s), and string([]byte) allocate and copy the data because strings are immutable.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Converting a float to an int rounds it.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It truncates toward zero: int(2.9) is 2 and int(-2.9) is -2. Use math.Round first if you want rounding.

visualExplorer.title: How a conversion T(v) flows
visualExplorer.caption: Follow a value as it crosses type boundaries: numeric widening, truncation, the rune trap, and strconv for real text.

config.intro: Go forces every cross-type move through an explicit T(v). Walk through what each kind of conversion actually does to the bits.

steps.name: 1. Widening: int to int64
steps.detail: int64(x) sign-extends the value into a wider box. No data is lost; the compiler still requires you to write it explicitly.

steps.name: 2. float to int truncates
steps.detail: int(2.9) drops the fractional part toward zero, giving 2. There is no rounding — math.Round(2.9) would be needed first to get 3.

steps.name: 3. Narrowing overflows
steps.detail: int8(300) keeps only the low 8 bits, wrapping to 44 by two's-complement truncation. Range-check untrusted values before narrowing.

steps.name: 4. The string(n) rune trap
steps.detail: string(65) reinterprets 65 as a Unicode code point and yields "A", not "65". For decimal text you must use strconv.Itoa.

steps.name: 5. strconv for text <-> number
steps.detail: strconv.Atoi("42") parses text into an int (with an error); strconv.Itoa(42) formats an int back into "42". This is the correct number<->string bridge.

interactiveExamples.title: Truncation, overflow, and the rune trap
interactiveExamples.explanation: Three classic surprises in one program: float-to-int truncates (not rounds), narrowing wraps, and string(n) gives a rune — not the digits.

code.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	f := 2.9
	fmt.Println(int(f))          // truncates toward zero -> 2

	big := 300
	fmt.Println(int8(big))       // keeps low 8 bits -> 44 (wraps)

	fmt.Println(string(rune(65))) // code point 65 -> "A", NOT "65"
}

interactiveExamples.title: Edit it: print "42", not a strange symbol
interactiveExamples.explanation: string(n) interprets n as a Unicode code point, so string(42) is a control character, not "42". Edit the code to print the decimal text using strconv.

checkpoints.explanation: Float-to-int conversion truncates toward zero, dropping the fractional part. -2.9 becomes -2, not -3. Rounding would require math.Round first.
string(rune(n)) converts a code point to its character: 72 is 'H' and 105 is 'i', so the result is "Hi". This is exactly why string(intVal) does NOT give you the decimal digits.

checkpoints.prompt: How do you correctly turn the int 255 into the string "255"?
checkpoints.explanation: strconv.Itoa formats an int as its decimal text. string(255) would give the rune for code point 255 ('y' with diaeresis), and []byte(255) does not compile.

checkpoints.code:
var i int = 10
var j int64 = 20
sum := i + j
fmt.Println(sum)

You cannot add two integers in Go
sum must be declared with var
checkpoints.explanation: Go has no implicit numeric conversions: int and int64 are different types and can't be mixed in an expression. You must convert one explicitly, e.g. sum := int64(i) + j.

codeLab.title: A type-safe temperature converter
codeLab.instructions: Defined types Celsius and Fahrenheit (both float64) are given. Implement `CToF(c Celsius) Fahrenheit` using the formula F = C*9/5 + 32. You'll need explicit conversions between the defined types and float64 to do the arithmetic and return the right type.
hints: Celsius and Fahrenheit are distinct types even though both are float64 underneath — you must convert explicitly.
Do the arithmetic in float64: float64(c)*9/5 + 32.
Wrap the final float64 result back into Fahrenheit(...) so the return type matches.

debuggingLab.title: Converting an int to a string gives a weird symbol
debuggingLab.symptom: The program is supposed to log "order #42" but prints "order #*" (or some other odd character) instead of the number.

brokenCode.code:
id := 42
msg := "order #" + string(rune(id)) // intended to append "42"
fmt.Println(msg)

debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: string(rune(id)) converts the integer to the Unicode character at that code point. Code point 42 is '*', so you get "order #*" instead of "order #42". Converting an int directly to a string never produces its decimal digits.
commonMistakes: Using string(intVal) (or string(rune(intVal))) expecting the decimal text.
Forgetting that strconv (or fmt.Sprintf) is the tool for number-to-text formatting.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Format the integer as decimal text with strconv.Itoa before concatenating.

solution.code:
import "strconv"

id := 42
msg := "order #" + strconv.Itoa(id) // Itoa -> "42"
fmt.Println(msg)

theory.question: Why does Go require explicit conversions like int64(x) even between integer types?
theory.directAnswer: Go has no implicit numeric conversions by design. Different numeric types are genuinely different types, and Go refuses to silently widen or narrow them because that's where C-style truncation and sign bugs hide. Forcing T(v) makes every boundary visible and turns potential runtime data loss into a compile-time decision.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A language rule that values of different types — even int and int64 — cannot be mixed in expressions or assigned without an explicit conversion.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To eliminate the implicit coercions that cause silent precision loss and overflow bugs in languages like C.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The compiler checks types statically; a mismatch is an error, and the only way through is an explicit conversion the programmer writes.

theory.whyImportant: It's a core philosophy question that reveals whether a candidate understands Go's safety-through-explicitness trade-off.
theory.realWorldExample: A database driver returns int64 ids; converting to int with int(id) makes the truncation risk on 32-bit platforms explicit instead of silent.

followUps.question: Is int64(x) free at runtime?
followUps.answer: For widening it's a single sign-extend instruction, effectively free. Narrowing is also cheap but may lose high bits.

followUps.question: Does the same rule apply to untyped constants?
followUps.answer: No — untyped constants like 5 adapt to the context's type automatically, so var f float64 = 5 needs no conversion.

theory.question: What's the difference between a type conversion T(v) and a type assertion x.(T)?
theory.directAnswer: A conversion T(v) is a compile-time operation between statically compatible types (numbers, defined types, []byte/string) that always succeeds. A type assertion x.(T) is a runtime operation on an interface value that extracts the concrete type, can fail (panic, or return ok=false in the comma-ok form), and only applies to interfaces. They look similar but solve different problems.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Conversion repackages a known concrete type; assertion inspects what concrete type hides inside an interface.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Conversions bridge compatible representations; assertions recover static type info that was erased when a value was stored in an interface.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The compiler resolves conversions statically. Assertions check the interface's dynamic type descriptor at runtime.

theory.whyImportant: Confusing the two is common; interviewers use it to test understanding of Go's type system and interfaces (a separate topic, golang-intermediate-4).
theory.realWorldExample: float64(i) converts an int; v, ok := any.(string) asserts that an interface{} actually holds a string before using it.

followUps.question: What happens if a type assertion fails without the comma-ok form?
followUps.answer: It panics at runtime. Use the v, ok := x.(T) form to handle the failure gracefully.

theory.question: What does converting a float to an int do in Go, and how is it different from rounding?
theory.directAnswer: int(f) truncates toward zero — it drops the fractional part rather than rounding to the nearest integer. So int(2.9) is 2 and int(-2.9) is -2, not 3 and -3. If you actually want rounding you have to call math.Round (or math.Floor/Ceil) first and then convert the result to int.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A numeric conversion that repackages a floating-point value into an integer type by discarding everything after the decimal point.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Truncation toward zero is a cheap, fully defined operation that maps directly to hardware float-to-int instructions, so Go picks it as the conversion semantics rather than a more expensive rounding rule.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: int(f) takes the whole-number part in the direction of zero; the sign is preserved and no bankers'/nearest rounding is applied.

theory.whyImportant: Assuming conversion rounds is a classic off-by-one source in pricing, pagination, and metrics code, and interviewers use it to check that a candidate knows Go's exact semantics.
theory.realWorldExample: Computing an average rating as int(sum/count) silently floors 4.9 to 4; wrapping it as int(math.Round(sum/count)) fixes the displayed value.

followUps.question: What happens if the float is out of the int range, like int(1e20)?
followUps.answer: The result is implementation-defined for out-of-range floats; you should range-check or use a wider type before converting untrusted magnitudes.

followUps.question: How would you round to the nearest integer instead?
followUps.answer: Convert with int(math.Round(f)); math.Round rounds halves away from zero, so 2.5 becomes 3.

theory.question: Why do []byte(s) and []rune(s) conversions allocate, and why should you avoid them in hot loops?
theory.directAnswer: Go strings are immutable, so converting a string to []byte or []rune cannot share the string's backing array — it must allocate a new slice and copy the data so the caller can mutate the slice safely. That copy is O(n) in time and memory, so doing it repeatedly inside a tight loop turns a cheap-looking conversion into a real allocation and GC pressure hotspot.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: String-to-slice conversions that produce a fresh, mutable copy of the underlying bytes or decoded runes.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Strings are read-only by contract; allowing []byte(s) to alias the string would let code mutate a supposedly immutable value, so the language copies instead.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The runtime allocates a new slice of the right length and memmoves the bytes (or decodes UTF-8 into runes for []rune), leaving the original string untouched.

theory.whyImportant: Conversion cost is a common performance interview topic; knowing which conversions allocate distinguishes numeric (free) from string (costly) conversions.
theory.realWorldExample: A parser that wrote for i := range s { b := []byte(s); ... } reallocated on every iteration; hoisting b := []byte(s) out of the loop cut allocations to one.

followUps.question: Can the compiler ever avoid the copy?
followUps.answer: Yes — the compiler optimizes common patterns like ranging over []byte(s) or using string([]byte) as a map key so no allocation actually happens.

followUps.question: How do []byte and []rune differ in cost?
followUps.answer: []byte copies raw bytes 1:1; []rune decodes UTF-8 into int32 code points, so it costs more per element and produces a slice whose length is the rune count, not the byte count.

scenario.question: A service reads a numeric count from an external system as int64, stores it in an int32 column-mapped field, and occasionally records show absurd negative counts. What's happening and how do you fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: The int64 is being narrowed to int32, and when the value exceeds the int32 range the conversion keeps only the low 32 bits via two's-complement truncation — which can flip the sign and produce a large negative number. The fix is to range-check before converting (reject or clamp values outside math.MinInt32..math.MaxInt32) or widen the field to int64.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Silent integer narrowing overflow at a type boundary.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Go defines narrowing as low-bit truncation, which is fast and predictable but lossy for out-of-range values.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: int32(largeInt64) discards the high bits; if bit 31 ends up set, the value is interpreted as negative.

scenario.whyImportant: Boundary narrowing is a real data-integrity bug class, especially with untrusted or growing external values.
scenario.realWorldExample: An event counter from a busy upstream exceeds 2.1 billion and wraps to a negative int32, corrupting dashboards and alerts.

followUps.question: How do you safely detect the overflow?
followUps.answer: Compare against math.MaxInt32/math.MinInt32 before converting, and return an error or clamp if out of range.

scenario.question: A teammate builds a message that should read "user 500 logged in" using "user " + string(id) + " logged in", but production logs show a strange box character where the number should be. What went wrong and how do you fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: string(id) converts the integer to the Unicode character at that code point, not to its decimal digits, so id 500 becomes the single rune U+01F4 ('ǔ'-region glyph) instead of "500". The fix is to format the number as text with strconv.Itoa(id) (or fmt.Sprintf("%d", id)) before concatenating. Modern go vet flags the int-to-string conversion as a warning.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The string(intVal) rune-conversion gotcha surfacing in log/message formatting.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: string(x) on an integer is defined to interpret x as a Unicode code point, a convenience for building strings from runes that traps people expecting decimal text.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: string(500) produces a one-rune string for code point 500; strconv.Itoa(500) instead walks the digits and produces the three-character string "500".

scenario.whyImportant: It is the single most famous conversion trap in Go and shows up constantly in logging, ID formatting, and message building.
scenario.realWorldExample: An audit log emitted an unprintable glyph for every order ID until the team replaced string(id) with strconv.Itoa(id), restoring readable "order 500" lines.

followUps.question: How does go vet help here?
followUps.answer: vet's stringintconv check reports conversions of an int to string, nudging you toward strconv.Itoa before the bug reaches production.

followUps.question: When is string(x) on an integer actually correct?
followUps.answer: When x is genuinely a rune/code point you want as a character, e.g. string(rune('A')) or building text from decoded runes.

systemDesign.question: You are designing the boundary layer of a Go service that ingests numeric IDs and counters from JSON APIs and a legacy database that uses 32-bit integer columns. How do you design the type-conversion strategy to keep data safe as it crosses these boundaries?
systemDesign.directAnswer: Standardize on the widest safe representation internally (int64) and make every narrowing conversion an explicit, validated step at the edge. JSON numbers decode to float64 by default, so parse IDs from strings or into json.Number and convert with strconv to avoid float precision loss above 2^53. At the DB boundary, range-check int64 values against int32 limits before converting, returning an error or clamping instead of silently truncating. Use defined types like UserID int64 so IDs can't be accidentally mixed with counts.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A layered conversion design where wide, precise types live in the core and narrowing/parsing happens only at validated boundaries.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Each boundary — JSON, DB, external API — has its own numeric representation, and Go's explicit conversions let you make every risky move (float precision loss, int32 narrowing, string parsing) visible and checkable.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Inbound: parse text/JSON with strconv or json.Number into int64. Internal: operate on int64 and domain-defined types. Outbound to a 32-bit column: check math.MinInt32..math.MaxInt32, then convert; reject or clamp out-of-range values.

systemDesign.whyImportant: Boundary conversions are where real services silently corrupt data — overflowed counters, truncated IDs, floats that lost precision — so a deliberate conversion strategy is a data-integrity design decision.
systemDesign.realWorldExample: A billing service decoded large invoice IDs as JSON float64 and lost the last digits above 2^53; switching to json.Number plus strconv.ParseInt into int64 preserved exact IDs across the whole pipeline.

followUps.question: Why is decoding large integer IDs as float64 dangerous?
followUps.answer: float64 exactly represents integers only up to 2^53; beyond that, IDs lose their least-significant digits, so two distinct IDs can collide.

followUps.question: How do defined types help at these boundaries?
followUps.answer: Types like UserID int64 and Count int64 are distinct despite the same underlying type, so the compiler stops you from passing a count where an ID is expected, catching mix-ups at compile time.

coding.question: Implement `func SumDigits(s string) (int, error)` that parses a string of digits like "12345" and returns the sum of its digit values, returning an error if the string isn't a valid integer.
coding.thoughtProcess: Parse the whole string to an int with strconv.Atoi (which returns an error for invalid input), then repeatedly take n%10 to peel off digits and n/=10 to shrink. Sum the remainders. Handle the empty/invalid case via the returned error.
coding.lineByLine: strconv.Atoi converts the text to an int and surfaces an error for non-numeric input. We take the absolute value so negatives still sum their digits. The loop pulls the last digit with %10, adds it, and divides by 10 to move on, stopping at 0. The error is propagated to the caller idiomatically.
coding.timeComplexity: O(d) where d is the number of digits

followUps.question: Why use strconv.Atoi instead of int(s)?
followUps.answer: int(s) doesn't compile — you can't convert a string to an int that way. strconv.Atoi is the correct text-to-number parser and reports invalid input.

followUps.question: How would you sum digits without parsing to int at all?
followUps.answer: Range over the string's runes and convert each digit rune with r - '0', validating each is between '0' and '9'.

coding.question: Implement `func NarrowToInt32(v int64) (int32, error)` that safely converts an int64 to int32, returning an error instead of silently truncating when the value is out of range.
coding.thoughtProcess: Direct int32(v) would keep only the low 32 bits and can flip the sign, corrupting data. The safe pattern is to range-check against math.MinInt32 and math.MaxInt32 first; only if v fits do we perform the explicit conversion. Otherwise we return a descriptive error so the caller decides how to handle the boundary case.
coding.lineByLine: The guard compares v against the int32 bounds from the math package before any conversion. If v is outside [MinInt32, MaxInt32] we return a zero value and an error naming the offending value. Only when v is proven to fit do we perform the explicit int32(v) conversion, which is now guaranteed lossless. The error return makes the boundary decision the caller's responsibility instead of silently wrapping.

followUps.question: What does int32(v) do without the check when v is 3000000000?
followUps.answer: It keeps only the low 32 bits via two's-complement truncation, producing a large negative number and silently corrupting the value.

followUps.question: Why use math.MinInt32/MaxInt32 instead of hardcoded literals?
followUps.answer: The named constants document intent and are correct regardless of platform, avoiding magic numbers like 2147483647 that are easy to mistype.

keyTakeaways: Go has no implicit numeric conversions — write T(v) explicitly, even between int and int64.
float-to-int truncates toward zero (not rounds), and narrowing keeps only the low bits, wrapping predictably.
string(n) yields the rune for code point n, not its digits — use strconv.Itoa / strconv.Atoi for number<->text.
[]byte(s) and []rune(s) allocate and copy; type conversion (compile-time) is distinct from a type assertion (runtime on interfaces).
